description_ru: Рассказ о первом обнаружении гравитационных волн: как устроен детектор LIGO и почему этот способ наблюдения изменил астрономию.
text:
On the fourteenth of September 2015, two detectors in the United States, one in Louisiana and one in Washington State, registered a tiny disturbance lasting a fraction of a second. The signal, later named GW150914, was the first direct detection of gravitational waves, ripples in the fabric of spacetime that Albert Einstein had predicted a century earlier. The event that produced them was a collision between two black holes, roughly thirty-six and twenty-nine times the mass of the Sun, more than a billion light years away.

According to general relativity, mass and energy curve spacetime, and an accelerating mass sends out waves in that curvature, much as a boat sends ripples across a pond. Most of the time these waves are impossibly faint. Even a violent cosmic event such as the merger of black holes stretches and squeezes the distance between objects on Earth by less than the width of a proton. Einstein himself doubted that we would ever be able to measure them.

The instruments that succeeded, known collectively as LIGO, are L-shaped and four kilometres on each side. A laser beam is split in two, sent down both arms, reflected by mirrors, and recombined. If the arms are exactly the same length, the light waves cancel out and the detector stays dark. A passing gravitational wave, however, stretches one arm very slightly while it shortens the other, and a trace of light appears. Achieving the necessary sensitivity took decades of engineering: the mirrors hang on slender glass fibres, and the whole apparatus sits in one of the largest vacuums ever created, shielded from vibrations as slight as distant traffic or ocean waves.

Because the two detectors lie thousands of kilometres apart, the signal reached them a few milliseconds apart, which allowed astronomers to estimate roughly the direction it came from. With additional detectors in Europe and Japan, the position can now be narrowed considerably, and the data have revealed a whole population of black holes that we had never seen.

Perhaps the most significant consequence is a change in how we observe the universe. For millennia, astronomy relied entirely on light. Gravitational waves are a different kind of messenger, passing through matter essentially unimpeded, and carrying information about events that no telescope could ever see. In 2017, detectors recorded the merger of two neutron stars. Within seconds a burst of gamma rays was detected, and within hours conventional telescopes around the world turned to watch the afterglow. That one collision helped explain where much of the universe's gold is forged. Listening, it turns out, has opened a window as profound as looking ever did.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: ˌsensiˈtivity, ˌunimˈpeded, asˈtronomers. Главное ударение падает на предпоследний слог перед -ity.
Долгий нейтральный звук: губы расслаблены, язык в центре; не произносите «ер» с русским «р».
Кончик языка слегка между зубами, звук глухой; не «с», «т» или «ф».
Дифтонг: от открытого «а» к «у», губы округляются в конце; не заканчивайте на «в».

questions.question: What did the detectors register in September 2015?
questions.answer: Gravitational waves from the collision of two black holes.

questions.question: How long are the arms of LIGO?
Why are there two detectors far apart?
questions.answer: The signal arrives at slightly different times, which shows its direction.

questions.question: What happened in 2017?
questions.answer: Detectors recorded the merger of two neutron stars.
